major.label: Major
major.description: Built on the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of the major scale, major chords have a bright, happy sound. When you see just a letter name like "C" or "G" with no suffix, it's a major chord.

m.label: Minor
m.description: The 3rd note is lowered by one half step, giving minor chords a darker, sadder sound compared to major chords. The "m" after the letter means the middle note is lowered, creating a melancholic feel.

7.label: Dominant 7th
7.description: A major chord with a flatted 7th note added, creating a bluesy tension that wants to resolve. It's the foundation of blues and jazz — a chord that sounds "unfinished" on purpose.

m7.label: Minor 7th
m7.description: A minor chord with a flatted 7th note added, combining the sadness of minor with the sophistication of the 7th. The result is a smooth, jazzy, warm sound used in neo-soul, R&B, and lo-fi music.

5.label: Power Chord
5.description: Contains only the root and 5th — no 3rd — making it neither major nor minor. Power chords are the backbone of rock and punk guitar, perfect for heavy distortion where full chords would sound muddy.

sus4.label: Suspended 4th
sus4.description: The 3rd is replaced by the 4th note, creating a tense, open sound that's neither happy nor sad. "Sus" stands for "suspended" — the chord hangs in the air, wanting to resolve.

add9.label: Added 9th
add9.description: A major chord with the 9th note (the 2nd note up an octave) layered on top without replacing anything. The 9th adds a shimmering, dreamy quality — like a richer version of the major chord.

add11.label: Added 11th
add11.description: A chord with the 11th note (the 4th up an octave) layered on top. The 11th adds an ethereal, open quality that's popular in modern acoustic and ambient music.

6/9.label: Six-Nine
6/9.description: A chord with both the 6th and 9th notes added, creating a lush, jazzy voicing that sounds complete and sophisticated. Popular in bossa nova and R&B.

7sus4.label: Dominant 7th Suspended 4th
7sus4.description: A dominant 7th chord where the 3rd is replaced by the 4th, combining bluesy 7th tension with the unresolved floating quality of a sus4. Double the tension, double the drama.

slash.label: Slash Chord
slash.description: The note after the "/" is played as the bass note instead of the root. The letter before the slash is the chord, and the letter after is the lowest note, creating smooth bass line movement between chords.

stuck34.label: Stuck 3 & 4
stuck34.description: Fingers 3 (ring) and 4 (pinky) stay "stuck" on strings 1 & 2 at fret 3 while other fingers change shape. This creates a beautiful drone effect — two notes ringing throughout chord changes.

4finger.label: 4-Finger Voicing
4finger.description: An alternate voicing that uses all four fretting fingers instead of three, adding an extra note for a richer, more complete sound.

open.label: Open Voicing
open.description: A voicing that leaves extra strings ringing open, creating a spacious, airy sound. The open strings act as drones that add harmonic richness.

var.label: Variation
var.description: An alternate fingering of the same chord that may use fewer fingers, different positions, or omit notes to create a slightly different tone color or make transitions easier.

full.label: Full Voicing
full.description: A voicing that includes more notes than the basic shape, producing a thicker, more resonant sound with more strings ringing.

groups.title: Major
groups.subtitle: The foundation of Western music — major chords produce a bright, happy sound. These open-position shapes are the first chords every guitarist learns and appear in virtually every genre from pop and rock to country and folk. Mastering these unlocks thousands of songs.

groups.title: Minor
groups.subtitle: Minor chords deliver a darker, more melancholic tone compared to their major counterparts. Essential for creating emotional depth in music, they are used extensively in rock ballads, blues, folk, and classical guitar. Every songwriter reaches for minor chords to convey sadness, tension, or introspection.

groups.title: Dominant 7th
groups.subtitle: Born in jazz and blues, dominant 7th chords add a bluesy tension that wants to resolve. They're the secret sauce behind 12-bar blues progressions and are heard in jazz standards, funk, R&B, and classic rock. Adding the flatted 7th note gives these chords their characteristic 'unfinished' quality.

groups.title: Minor 7th
groups.subtitle: Minor 7th chords blend the moodiness of minor chords with the sophistication of the 7th, creating a smooth, jazzy sound. They're staples in neo-soul, R&B, bossa nova, and lo-fi music. These chords add warmth and complexity without sounding harsh.

groups.title: Power Chords
groups.subtitle: Power chords contain only the root and fifth — no third — making them neither major nor minor. This ambiguity is what makes them perfect for rock, punk, metal, and grunge where heavy distortion would turn a full chord into mush. Movable up and down the neck, they're the backbone of electric guitar.

groups.title: Stuck 3&4
groups.subtitle: Named because fingers 3 and 4 stay 'stuck' on the thinnest two strings at the 3rd fret, these chord shapes produce a beautiful drone effect — two notes ringing out together throughout chord changes. Popularized in songs like Wonderwall, they give acoustic guitar a rich, shimmering quality. Expect your pinky to get a workout!
